title: How can I get into avant garde?

commenti.body:
I'm not sure what you need, but here is a list from the Soviet cinema avantgarde:  
The Soviet cinema avant-garde is a trend in the art of the 1920s and 1930s, which is characterized by the search for new means of artistic expression and experiments with editing. The direction was closely connected with the renewal of art after the revolution, and many of its representatives were engaged, among other things, in the analysis of the film language.  
"Battleship Potemkin"  
1925, dir. Sergey Eisenstein  
A historical and revolutionary blockbuster about the uprising on the ship  
One of the main films of the Soviet 1920s and the entire history of cinema. Using as a starting point one of the episodes of the 1905 revolution — the uprising on the battleship Prince Potemkin-Tavrichesky — Eisenstein managed to shoot a clear and at the same time multi-layered picture of the brotherhood. Viewers of "Potemkin" from different countries and eras found in the film both a call to fight social injustice and an allegory full of Christian symbols about the battle with the troops of the "prince of this world". This innovative picture, in which the author actively experiments with editing, abandons a specific main character and makes his character a multifaceted mass. And it's also just a fascinating film that makes the viewer squirm in his chair more than once (review at least the scene of the destruction of the demonstration on the Potemkin stairs — it's scary!).  
"Mother"  
1926, dir. Vsevolod Pudovkin  
A realistic drama about the rise of revolutionary consciousness  
Based on the novel of the same name by Maxim Gorky, which by that time already had a classic status, Pudovkin and screenwriter Nathan Zarkhi create their own work. The story of positive revolutionaries turns into a fascinating story with a rebellion against a despotic father and the gradual epiphany of an unhappy, downtrodden woman. Both themes will turn out to be extremely important for the Soviet cinema of the 1920s, and "Mother" will be declared the fundamental picture for the subsequent Soviet cinema. Pudovkin proposed his own theory of editing, the opposite of Eisenstein's: frames should not collide, but line up in a coherent narrative. But for all its realism, "Mother" uses poetic metaphors (in the finale, the revolution is rhymed with a spring ice breaker) and works subtly with the frame (the evolution of the heroine's consciousness is shown using a series of expressive close-ups).  
"The Man with the movie Camera"  
1929, dir. Dziga Vertov  
A documentary portrait of the city and a hymn to the possibilities of the film language  
Unlike Eisenstein or Pudovkin, Vertov believed that the future of cinema belongs to non-fiction films, because reality is much more exciting than any, the most fantastic inventions. To prove his point, Vertov creates the "Man with a Movie Camera" — an exhibition of achievements of the Soviet school of cinematography (sharp angles, combined shooting, hand-held camera and shooting in motion). This "experience of the complete separation of the language of cinema from the language of theater and literature, devoid of any ideological touch," shows that the everyday life around us, caught by surprise by a skilled cinematographer, really turns out to be an exciting spectacle. Vertov, who shot in Moscow, Kiev and Odessa, erects a monument to the entire urban civilization of the 1920s and, with the help of editing documentary footage, creates a new reality that exists only on film.  
"Earth"  
1930, dir. Alexander Dovzhenko  
Poetic cinema about communism as a natural element  
Formally, Dovzhenko makes films about a tractor and a collective farm, against the kulaks and the church, but "Earth" least of all resembles dull propaganda. Communism here is embedded in an almost religious system of a new joyful paganism, in which a tractor, an airplane, apples, pears and ears of wheat full of grain are all a product of Mother earth, and a murdered Komsomol member will surely rise after the autumn rains, as grain dropped into the ground is revived. And Dovzhenko's revolutionary shooting style (long plans instead of fast-changing shots) had a strong influence on the development of Soviet cinema in the 1930s.  
"The Women of Ryazan"  
1927, dir. Olga Preobrazhenskaya, Ivan Pravov  
A SOCIAL DRAMA ABOUT VIOLENCE IN THE PATRIARCHY  
The heroine becomes a victim of violence by her father-in-law, gives birth to a child and takes her own life. Her sister—in-law, who was expelled from the family, opens a nursery in an abandoned manor house in spite of everyone - as a symbol of the new village. The picture was met with massive success and discontent on the part of Eisenstein, who considered all this a step back to pre-revolutionary melodrama. "Women of Ryazan" looks relevant and fresh even now, and not only because of the topic of sexual harassment, shot with painful truthfulness by a female director. Olga Preobrazhenskaya and Ivan Pravov, who shot their drama on location, found an accurate and expressive language for depicting village life, with an abundance of general plans and lyrical shots of nature. The mowing scene with figures of peasants inscribed in the landscape can be attributed to the most poetic moments of Soviet cinema of the 1920s. The "Women of Ryazan" were an important predecessor of Dovzhenko's "Land".  
"The White Eagle"  
1928, dir. Yakov Protazanov  
A HISTORICAL DRAMA FROM A CLASSIC OF PRE-REVOLUTIONARY CINEMA  
In the 1920s, Yakov Protazanov was not only not considered an avant-garde artist, but was directly opposed to the avant-garde. One of the leading directors of pre-revolutionary Russia, in the Soviet years he shot films intended for the "wide audience": folk comedies, melodramas about treacherous manufacturers and fiction about a flight to Mars. What could be further from the complex montage epics about the revolution and the Civil War? Nevertheless, Protazanov himself actively used all the achievements of the changing film language, which he demonstrated in his "White Eagle" — a film with a traditional avant-garde reflection on the pre-revolutionary past. The plot centers on the governor, a good man who must commit a bad deed. He will have to suppress the workers' demonstrations by force in order to end the strikes. Telling this story, Protazanov, on the one hand, relies on actors — the main roles in his film are played by the premier of the Moscow Art Theater Vasily Kachalov, theater director Vsevolod Meyerhold and Anna Stan, one of the main Soviet stars of the era. On the other hand, he uses editing techniques borrowed from the younger generation of Soviet directors: the mass scenes included in the "White Eagle" would do credit to the films of Pudovkin or Dovzhenko.  
"A Fragment of the Empire"  
1929, dir. Friedrich Ermler  
THE NEW STRUCTURE OF SOCIETY THROUGH THE EYES OF A PRE-REVOLUTIONARY SOLDIER  
Friedrich Ermler's film about a man who suffered a concussion during World War I and recovered in Soviet times fully reflected the confusion of the inhabitants of pre-revolutionary Russia in the new society. "The Fragment of the Empire" is interesting both by the play of the wonderful Moscow Art Theater actor Fyodor Nikitin, and by the installation, and by sudden poetic images. The episode of the return of memory, in which the sound of a sewing machine makes the hero recall machine-gun bursts from the war, can be attributed to one of the most powerful and memorable scenes of the Soviet avant-garde cinema.  
"Happiness"  
1934, dir. Alexander Medvedkin  
A splint story about the change of epochs  
One of the last great silent films shot in the Soviet Union. Its author is Alexander Medvedkin, a participant in the Civil War, a political instructor of the First Cavalry, a convinced communist. In his work, Medvedkin talked about the Soviet government, but his stories often turned out to be too accurate, and therefore unacceptable. So "Happiness," his first feature film, quickly ended up on the shelf. In fact, the film splits into two parts. In the first, brighter one, the peasant Hmyr is trying to find his happiness in a semi-mysterious pre-revolutionary Russia. Depicting his ordeal, Medvedkin actively resorts to folklore images, and to direct visualization of folk sayings like "One with a bipod — seven with a spoon", and to gags in the spirit of "The Simpsons" or "South Park" (oh, those nuns in their transparent robes!).  
The second part is less joyful. An evil fist is active in it, the main purpose of which is the destruction of all that is good in the world. Khmyr himself will lose his identity closer to the finale in order to become an ordinary Soviet citizen of the 1930s, ashamed of his past and laughing at the ragged starving exes. In this finale, which may seem rather harsh to a modern viewer, the onset of a new era is felt
Thank you so much for taking the time to write this

I don't have time right now to write more, but I would recommend studying Luis Buñuel as a historical way to access this type of cinema

You can start with the Buñuel-Dali collaboration "Un chien andalou" (An Andalusian Dog) 1929, which is possibly the first self-consciously artistic foray into film, in the sense that it has no recognisable narrative and doesn't adhere to any known theatrical convention - though this is and has been argued at length. 

There are lots of videos of this short film on YouTube, such as [this one](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W8yKT7H_KJ0). 

You could do worse than following Buñuel's extensive filmography from there. 

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis\_Bu%C3%B1uel\_filmography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Bu%C3%B1uel_filmography)

With 50 years of filmmaking there's a lot to get your teeth into there. If you want a beginner's guide, the BFI has a good one

[https://www.bfi.org.uk/features/where-begin-with-luis-bunuel](https://www.bfi.org.uk/features/where-begin-with-luis-bunuel)

In general the BFI is a great resource for guides, lists and easy-to-read critical pieces. 

That's all I have time for now, hope it helps.

Do not mention it. I copied more than I wrote

I'll probably mention three more films. Which, it seems to me, are close to the avant-garde

"Aelita" 1924. directed by Yakov Protazanova. This is a fantastic film, so I'm not sure that it can be directly attributed to the avant-garde, but its scenery and costumes are filled with constructivism.

The Tale of the Kibalchish Boy. 1964 Directed by Evgeny Sherstobitov. A film adaptation of a children's fairy tale by Arkady Gaidar.  
Because I can't write beautifully.... Photographer Ekaterina Pomelova writes: "The most powerful color scheme of the series refers us to the poster aesthetics of the 1920s, to such outstanding avant-garde artists as El Lisitsky or Rodchenko. The colorful extravaganza of all the visualizations of the fairy tale focuses on the production of only two images — the image of a valiant hero and the image of an absolute enemy."

"Intervention" is a film directed by Gennady Poloka, a performance buff, filmed in 1968.

The action takes place in March 1919; the Entente troops arrive in Odessa, which is under the rule of the Whites, with whom the opponents of the Bolsheviks pin great hopes.

As the director himself said, "embittered by the cliches accumulated by our "official cinema" in films about the civil war," in an interview he called for "reviving the traditions of theater and cinema of the first years of the revolution, the traditions of farcical, street, buffoonish performances."
Thank you, I've actually heard about him but I didn't know he made avant garde films.

Basically, the Buñuel, the Soviet stuff described in such excellent detail by Morozow (made a copy of that for my own reference), and a few French things like Cocteau's Orphée trilogy will give you a fine grounding in pre-war art cinema. 

So that's just the first 30 years or so. Should take about a year to get through that. 

Don't forget, the BFI is a great source for material on all kinds of cinema

https://www.bfi.org.uk/articles/type/features

https://www.bfi.org.uk/articles

[free database of avant garde film](https://www.ubu.com/film/)

Have fun exploring. I had to use this database in college. There’s plenty to here to check out. Just enter in the different artists names into google and see what style might appeal to you. 

I’ve never been crazy about experimental films. But there’s so many cool techniques these people pioneered that show up in mainstream films. 

Enjoy

I recently went through Flicker Alley's box set of (American) avant-garde cinema, which consists of 30+ films. I feel like it would make a good introduction as it includes many famous films that you'd study in film classes and it organizes the films in chronological order. There's a good variety of animation, expressionism, surrealism, city symphony, experiential, etc. The best part is that they're all short films, so it'll be easier to commit to than a feature film. Not saying you ought to buy the blu-ray, but I would recommend using the list as a guide. Hope this helps!
https://re-voir.com/shop/en/film-revoir-experiemental-film-dvd/814-masterworks-of-american-avant-garde-experimental-film-1920-1970.html

Most modern art museums have a film department.  You can go to the one close to you and find out.  If you are in New York City, there are Avant Garde film programs going on every so often.  You can catch works by Michael Snow, Stan Brakhage, and Ernie Gehr.
